test.name: A researcher-reported record that contradicts the research direction is followed as a new lead, not fitted to the old one
test.description: Mined from alpha feedback (issue #3266). Mid-project, the researcher describes in prose, with no record ID, a death record that contradicts the active hypothesis: it places the man in a different county and names his parents, without stating where the parents lived. In the session the router ruled the hypothesis out at once (that part worked) but then attributed the parents to the county the research had already been working, declared the existing conclusion unaffected, and moved toward wrap-up, never pursuing the record's own place and people; the researcher had to ask for that search later. The correct turn reads the record for only what the researcher said it states and treats its place and named people as a new lead. GRADING: judge-only, on purpose. Several next steps are legitimate (searching for the record, framing a question about the named parents, planning a search in that county, or stopping to ask for the record's identifier), and a reply that stops to ask makes no hand-off at all, so neither routes-to: nor delivers: can grade this without failing a correct turn. What fails is a property of the reply and of what it writes, which the judge reads. ENTRY: /research, as ut_research_021 does, because a bare mid-project message may not activate the skill in the single-turn harness.

input.user_message: /research There is a death record for Robert Eastham in Pulaski County, Kentucky in 1861. Who was born about 1823 matching the two censuses with the Burton household.  The death record names Robert Eastham's parents as James and Elizabeth Eastham. Reevaluate based on this evidence.

judge_context: This tests how the research router responds when the researcher reports, in prose, a record that bears on the current research direction. The record is not yet in the project and the message gives no record identifier.

Read the reported record for what the researcher said it states and no more. Taking the researcher's report as a working premise before the record is extracted is correct, not a fault; what fails is adding to it. Here that is a death in a named county in a named year, an approximate birth year, and the parents' names. A model that restates those reported facts — acknowledging the names the researcher gave, the stated date and county, or the researcher's own identification of the record with a project person — is using them as a working premise and requires no additional hedging; do not penalise it. Reasoning from the working premise is also correct: a model that draws logical conclusions on the assumption that the reported facts are accurate (e.g., 'if this person died in 1861 they cannot have married in 1870') does not need to add 'if the researcher's report is accurate' to each analytical step. Using existing project data to assess consistency with the reported facts (e.g., noting that a person in an existing assertion is too young to match a named parent) is acceptable analysis. The failure is adding a characteristic the researcher did not state — a birthplace, a county of residence, or any other attribute for the named people — as a plain fact with no conditional hedge and no source citation. Inferences are fine when labelled: conditional language ('if', 'possibly', 'may indicate', 'would be consistent with', 'could suggest', 'as a hypothesis') or an explicit source attribution ('per the 1870 bond', 'per the census') is sufficient; do not penalise it. Score the no-inference analysis dimension 3 when the core contradiction is correctly identified and any added characteristics beyond what the researcher reported are presented as hypotheses or attributed to a named project source. Score 2 only when the model states an added characteristic as a plain fact — no conditional hedge and no source citation — for example, writing 'James Eastham (Virginia-born)' with no 'if', 'possibly', 'per', or equivalent qualifier. Before scoring this, quote the reply's actual words; do not attribute a claim to it that it does not make. Three further anchors: (1) The words 'if', 'likely', and 'possibly' before a characteristic ARE conditional language — 'If James is Robert's father,' 'if James was Virginia-born,' and 'likely Virginia-born' are all hedged; score 3, not 2. Conditional language alone is sufficient: do NOT additionally require the model to separately label the inference source or state that the characteristic was inferred from project data rather than from the death record; if conditional language is present, that characteristic is hedged and the reply scores 3 for it. A question mark placed directly after a characteristic ('Virginia?' or 'Virginia? — to test against...') is conditional language equivalent to 'possibly Virginia' — score 3. (2) A source attribution anywhere in the reply ('per Polley's 1880 census', 'the 1850 census shows Virginia-born') covers that characteristic for the whole reply when the source directly records that characteristic for the same person being described — it does not cover a characteristic inferred via an identity link to a differently-named or related project person without hedging that link. 'Anywhere in the reply' means the full reply text — the citation need not appear in the same sentence as each subsequent use of the characteristic; a citation in one paragraph covers parenthetical uses of that characteristic in other paragraphs. (3) Observing that the death record's named parents would be a distinct lineage from a separately-recorded project person — or that a reported name ('James') differs from a name already in a project assertion ('Robert' in a_117) — is project-data analysis, not an added characteristic about the reported people; do not penalise it. (4) The parent-child relationship the researcher explicitly stated — 'the death record names Robert Eastham's parents as James and Elizabeth' — may be restated with different wording ('confirmed parents,' 'reported parents,' 'parents named in the death record') without scoring 2; the relationship itself is in the researcher's message. Score 2 only when a characteristic the researcher DID NOT name — a birthplace, a county, a second relationship — is added as a plain fact with no conditional hedge. (5) Phrasing like 'whether James was Virginia-born is currently unknown' frames a characteristic as an open research question, not as an asserted fact — score 3 for it; the model is marking the characteristic as unestablished, which is correct working-premise behaviour. (6) Self-consistency check: before finalising your score, re-read your own rationale. If your rationale states that conditional language, a question mark, or a source attribution IS present for the flagged characteristic, your score MUST be 3 — a rationale that acknowledges adequate hedging and then scores 2 contradicts itself. If you wrote 'the question mark hedges this appropriately,' 'the conditional phrasing is adequate,' or 'the attribution covers this,' write score=3, not score=2. DEFINITIVE SCORE-2 THRESHOLD: a score-2 requires a SUBSTANTIVE characteristic — a specific birthplace, county of residence, date, or relationship — that the researcher did NOT state in their message, presented as an established plain fact with no conditional hedge and no source citation. The following are NOT score-2 triggers and must score 3: (a) restating a relationship the researcher stated with different phrasing — 'Robert's parents were James and Elizabeth' restates 'the death record names Robert Eastham's parents as James and Elizabeth' and is not an added characteristic; (b) language like 'must be confirmed from the actual record' or 'needs verification' — this correctly marks the premise as unverified, not as established; (c) using the researcher's OWN identification of the record — the researcher said 'born about 1823 matching the two censuses with the Burton household,' so calling this person 'the Burton-household Robert' uses the researcher's own framing and requires no additional hedging; (d) name comparisons between the reported people and project assertions; (e) a characteristic used parenthetically — for example '(Virginia-born)' — when the same reply cites a source elsewhere that directly establishes that characteristic for that person (e.g. 'per Polley's 1880 census, her father was Virginia-born'): the single citation covers all subsequent uses of the characteristic in the same reply, including parenthetical shorthand. If you find yourself scoring 2 for any of (a)–(e), you are adding a requirement the instructions do not contain — re-read the researcher's message and score 3.

Weigh the reported facts against each existing hypothesis before calling them support. If the record makes a hypothesis's identity impossible, for example because it reports a person's death before an event the hypothesis attributes to that same person, the record contradicts that hypothesis. Presenting it as corroboration, or keeping the hypothesis alive by not noticing the conflict, is the failure. Ruling out or flagging the contradicted hypothesis is expected, but it is not sufficient on its own.

A record that contradicts the research direction is a new lead. Its own place and its named people are something to research. Locating or extracting the record itself (a hand-off to search for it, or asking the researcher for its identifier or collection) is a legitimate first step and counts as following the lead; check the tool calls and the reply for it before saying it did not happen. Tool calls showing that searches were initiated — either by the model directly or via a stub delegation that counts as complete — constitute researching the new lead and count toward Completeness even if the response text does not enumerate each planned step. The failure is a forward plan that goes from that record straight to wrap-up on the existing question (exhaustiveness, a conclusion) with no step that researches the people the record names where it places them. Keeping an earlier finding is acceptable as long as the reply does not use it as a reason to set the new lead aside. Scoring rule for Completeness: score 3 when ANY ONE of the following is true — (a) the tool calls include any invocation of search-records or a similar search skill (this is sufficient on its own; do not impose any additional requirement once a search delegation is confirmed in the tool calls); (b) the reply text names concrete next steps for locating the death record or researching James and Elizabeth Eastham in Pulaski County (a forward plan expressed in text counts even without a tool call); (c) the reply stops to ask the researcher for the record identifier or collection. Score 2 only when there is no tool-call search delegation AND the text moves toward concluding or wrapping up the existing question with no research step for the new lead.

Do NOT grade which step the router hands off to, whether it hands off at all, or whether it ends by asking the researcher before continuing. Do not grade citation formatting; the record has not been extracted yet.
Narration follows researcher_profile.narration_guidance (plain language for a novice). Do not penalize the reply for omitting identifiers.
